name: Saved passwords and autofill data
plain: Pages cannot read passwords or addresses saved in the browser.
meaning: Password managers fill on user action or after an autofill choice. Known weak spot: hidden-field autofill attacks and the :autofill CSS pseudo-class, which reveals that a field was autofilled (a boolean), but never the value before user action.

access.persistence: read fresh on every page load; nothing stored
access.iframe: Readable from cross-origin iframes too (same values)

fields.name: proxy: :autofill pseudo-class
fields.range: styling hook shows a field was autofilled

fields.name: proxy: Credential Management get()
fields.range: mediated by a prompt for stored credentials of that origin only

limits.headline: Can't see passwords or addresses saved in your browser
limits.user_action: You tap a field and choose a saved login or address to fill
can: Tell that a field was filled, using the autofill style check
Receive the value you choose to fill in
Ask the browser to offer a saved login
cannot: See saved addresses or cards before you choose
Get hidden fields filled before you choose, in most browsers
See which entries exist in your password manager
limits.reach_label: Only what you choose to fill

story.what_it_is: Pages cannot read passwords or addresses saved in your browser.

marketing.name: Chrome Password Manager
marketing.pitch: Google describes saving, filling and checking passwords in Chrome so you do not have to remember them.

story.for_you: A site cannot ask your browser for a list of your saved passwords. Your browser fills in a login only when you tap or confirm. A site just sees the filled field after that.
story.for_makers: Passwords and addresses are the most valuable data. Browsers fill only after a user action. There are some tricks, like hidden form fields that catch autofill, which vendors keep closing.

use_cases.example: A bank login page shows your saved login only when you tap the field and confirm.
A checkout page shows saved addresses after you pick one from the browser prompt.
A malicious page used hidden form fields to catch autofill data, which browsers now block.
A social site wanted all saved passwords to catch reuse and cannot.
A payment form shows a saved card after you approve it.
A developer builds login forms that work well with autofill.
A company portal wanted to see which sites use weak passwords and cannot.

risks: Autofill after you tap shows data to the page

legit_uses: None: the browser deliberately withholds it
